nameStory: Peanutgrass gets its quirky name from its unusual habit of producing two very different types of seeds - some above ground like normal grasses, and others below ground or near the soil surface, somewhat like peanuts! This double seed strategy is actually reflected in its scientific name 'amphicarpon,' which means 'double fruit' in Greek.
description: Peanutgrass is a relatively uncommon annual wetland grass that grows in small clumps or patches. It's a modest-sized grass that typically reaches 1-3 feet tall with narrow, flat leaves. What makes this grass special isn't flashy flowers or bright colors, but its sneaky survival strategy of making seeds both above and below ground - a rare trait among grasses.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Look for the telltale double seed production - small, typical grass seeds on open flower clusters above, plus larger, plumper seeds produced at or below ground level near the base of the plant

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Produces two distinct types of flower clusters: airy, open panicles (branched clusters) above ground with tiny, greenish flowers, and hidden, bead-like flowers near the soil surface

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, flat grass blades that feel smooth to the touch and emerge alternately from the stem, typically 2-6 inches long with a fresh, grassy scent when crushed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small, scattered clumps rather than dense mats, with stems that may bend or lean rather than standing perfectly upright

habitat: Peanutgrass thrives in wet, sandy soils of marshes, pond edges, and seasonal wetlands throughout New England. You'll most likely spot it in areas that flood seasonally but dry out partially in summer, often growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other wetland grasses. It prefers full sun to partial shade in these marshy environments.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin growing their first narrow leaves, looking like typical young grass shoots in wet areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when you can observe both types of flowering - the visible panicles above ground and the hidden flowers near the base that will become underground seeds.
seasonality.fall: Plants mature their double seed crop and begin to yellow and die back, leaving behind their unique two-part seed legacy in the soil.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants have died back completely, leaving no above-ground trace, but their buried seeds wait in the wet soil for spring.

funFact: Peanutgrass is one of only a handful of grasses in North America that hedge their bets by making two completely different types of seeds - if the above-ground seeds get eaten by birds or washed away in floods, the buried 'insurance policy' seeds are still safe underground to sprout next year!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other small wetland grasses, but the key is looking for evidence of that double seed production - check around the base of the plant for the larger, plumper seeds hiding near or below the soil surface while other grasses only have seeds up top.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, peanutgrass is not related to actual peanuts at all - it's a true grass that just happens to share the peanut's strategy of putting some seeds underground. The alternative name 'Pursh's blue maidencane' honors Frederick Pursh, an early American botanist who helped catalog many native plants.
compareHints: Since peanutgrass is the only species in its genus Amphicarpum found in New England, compare it to other small wetland grasses in the broader grass family. Unlike most wetland grasses that only produce seeds in obvious flower heads, peanutgrass stands alone with its sneaky double seed system. Other wetland grasses like wild rice or reed grasses are typically much taller and only make seeds above ground.
